Ghost Squad

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cape Town gets tough

Summary:
It's been six years since the Ghost Squad made its debut on Cape Town roads. These are a fleet of unmarked very fast cars with expert traffic officer drivers who spend their time roaming the streets, night and day, nabbing offenders - drivers who make mistakes, reckless drivers, speeding, jumping robots etc. We review how successful they have been and we meet their latest vehicle bought specifically to chase down illegal drag racers. This year 12 have been arrested so far and on Saturday they intend to pounce again. We will have John Webb and JP Smith in the car with two GO PROS.

Apparently there is a R5000 fund set up by these illegal racers and that goes to whoever is able to outrun the new ghost squad car - a powerful Pessatt costing R800 000.

Further information:
But there is more to the story and we must laud the Western Cape for taking draconious action to reduce the fatalities in the province. When people run from the police ie are chased in a motor vehicle, all they can be charged with is reckless driving. That soon is about to change with imminent new legislation which allows police officers to impound vehicles and stiffer penalties which allow for imprisonment.

Jump a red robot and you are slapped with a R15 000 fine. If your car is not licensed, another R1500. If you don't have your license on you you can be taken to the police station and wait their till a relative brings it. But most important is that Cape Town, within the next couple of months is about to unveil a private blood laboratory which will test blood scientifically on an alleged drunken driver and the very net day the blood results will be available in court. Normally there is about a nine month waiting period. This has the backing of private funders. It is clear from all of this that Cape Town is bent on stamping out drunken and reckless driving.

Press Release:


Cape Town Ghost Squad
Speedsters beware. With their new high-tech spy car, Cape Town’s Ghost Squad is set to haunt reckless drivers and illegal street racers. But can they outsmart the city’s notorious night-time drifters and dicers? Carte Blanche hitches a ride.


Script:


SOUND UP: "I've got both vehicles speeding down Strandfontein Road. Directions fine."

It’s a growing subculture in Cape Town, illegal street racing and it has authorities exasperated. but soon new legislation will be introduced to try and curb these speedsters who literally dice with death.

LINK: One of the issues that really gets up the noses of the City of Cape Town's traffic authorities is illegal street racing but now they have these high powered, high performance cars which are more than capable of chasing down those petrol heads.

In THIS SHORT STREET ALONE WE came across THREE modified CARS USED FOR ILLEGAL DRAG RACING.

THIs student recently spent R9000 on a new exhaust system to achieve extra speed. The proud owner of this souped up Subaru is constantly monitoring his cell phone for details about the next event.

INTERVIEW DRAGSTER: It will happen maybe every second night. We get a phone call or you get an sms. You know how things happen.

We went out recently to see for ourselves, especially since we had heard that dragsters had put up a R5000 reward for one of their own if they could outrun the ghost squad. This officer, a ghost squad motorcyclist knows all about the dangers involved. Recently he and his colleague’s tried to set up a roadblock to prevent a race from taking place. Two dragsters flew past him.

INTERVIEW LLOYD MATTHEWS: I can remember the impact as it happened. I hit it on the side, okay, and the bike went out of control. The impact went on my head where I have this scar.

The dragster stopped his car, and did not bother to help Lloyd. He spun his wheels and sped off. Lloyd is recovering from reconstructive surgery

We arrived at a location at round midnight . Hundreds of spectators were already lining the streets waiting for the racing to start. We parked close by a set of traffic lights and then heard the roar as two dragsters let rip.

A high-speed chase ensued, leading to the arrest of two drivers who pleaded their innocence. They were taken to a local police station where they would spend the night before appearing in court the next day.

INTERVIEW JP SMITH: This goes on all night. We'll arrest a bunch, take them to the police station, the rest will carry unabated. It's like a school of minnows, the Orca comes through, grabs a bunch and the rest just watch it happen and carry on going.

Sure enough - the presence of the now recognisable ghost squad vehicles didn’t put a halt to the action. Here two cars try and block us as a race went on ahead. We passed the one dragster who would be stopped by another ghost squad car. We chased the other driver. Notice the massive accident that could have happened - there was car stranded on the street.

It was hair rising. Our driver, John Bezuidenhout reached a speed of 207 km per hour. This dragster could not outrun him and he eventually gave up. Several arrests followed.

New legislation is imminent – the evade and allude law which will see the impoundment of these dragster cars, crippling fines and even imprisonment of the drivers. Reckless driving was one of contributing factors to the more than 1200 deaths on Western Cape roads last year.

LINK: The Western Cape Government is set to introduce sweeping new legislation aimed at bringing that figure down.

For example repeat traffic offenders can see their cars impounded. Capetonians are already reeling from increased traffic fines – to name a few jumping a red robot R2000, crossing a barrier line R2500 , parking in a loading zone R800.

MEC Donald grant defends these hefty fines.

INTERVIEW DONALD GRANT: What happened was, actually there were no increases for ten year. So we've been playing catchup and the fines now are beginning to bite.

The highly successful ghost squad, a fleet of super fast unmarked police cars and motorcycles spends its day dishing out these fines to motorists who break the law. Established 5 years ago, they have arrested over 5000 motorists. They have their work cut out for them. We spent just 45 minutes with John Bezuidenhout who has the highest arrest rate.

INTERVIEW JOHN BEZUIDENHOUT: John W: So how many arrests are we talking about, John?
John B: Since I've been on the unit I've made just over 700 arrests.

This driver crosses lanes twice without indicating. That’s R500 a pop.

Watch this motorcyclist crossing the channel line. He was pulled over and fined R500.

The car coming up on the right was travelling at over 140 km's on a crowded highway. Watch how he dangerously he rushes up behind a slower car.

His excuse -. He was late for a meeting. That cost him R2500.


INTERVIEW JOHN BEZUIDENHOUT: John W: John how much money have you made in past 40 minutes for the city?
John B: Just over R4000.
John W: Thats not a bad 40 minutes work is it?
John B: No it's not.


These officers believe they are making a difference. Now the cost of road accidents on the sa economy is estimated at over 300 billion rand a year.

INTERVIEW DONALD GRANT: Our share of that in the Western Cape based on 2013 data was approximately 21 Billion which is more than our health budget which is just over 18 Billion.

And that’s not taking into account the immeasurable human cost. .


Up and coming Cape Town Singer, model and actor, Thabang Sidloyi, was travelling to Woodstock with friends in early December last year. He was especially proud of his starring role in the international film The Goodman.

UPSOUND

Apparently Thabang was asleep in the back seat, his car being driven by someone else - seemingly at high speeds.

INTERVIEW CIKIZWA SIDLOYI: They tried to stop him. They said they tried to stop him to tell him to calm down, slow down, slow down.

This footage was shot on a dash cam and sensitive viewers beware. The driver lost control……….and Thabang, not wearing his seatbelt was flung from the vehicle. He didn’t stand a chance. He died of his injuries leaving behind a devastated family.

INTERVIEW CIKIZWA SIDLOYI: I'm not doing well. I'm just trying to be strong for my family.

Thabang was Cikizwa's first born of 4 children. Especially hard hit has been his grandmom who doted on him. A face to another statistic, another senseless death on cape roads.

Those who insist on driving flat out have a safe and controlled environment to do so.. And that’s at the Killarney international race track just outside the city. The main track is available once a month. Drag races also take place monthly. Now the city of cape town is in negotiations with the track management to make these events more regular.

LINK: The turnout at this event is absolutely incredible but I suppose the immediate question is how many of these cars would be on the streets if they weren't on the track tonight.

Lots according to the dragsters we spoke to, who seem to enjoy their cat and mouse game with the ghost squad. The owner of the souped up Subaru is one such example.

INTERVIEW DRAGSTER: I've never been caught by the police. If they try, I will try and outrun them.

Perhaps illegal dragsters and other reckless drivers should heed the words of Thabang’s mother.

INTERVIEW CIKIZWA SIDLOYI: Even if maybe something is telling him inside that I am safe. But he must think of other people as well.

And understand the suffering their actions can cause.

INTERVIEW CIKIZWA SIDLOYI: Reckless driving has caused me like...I don't even know now that I will ever be the same, feel the same way I used to when my son was here.
